headline: Final rinse water you can defend in your cleaning validation and at your next MDSAP audit
lead: For most devices the last thing to touch the product before packaging is water. Endotoxin and bioburden left by that rinse count against the device: USP <161> sets 20.0 EU per device, and 2.15 EU per device for cerebrospinal fluid contact, and the bioburden you measure to ISO 11737-1 sets your sterilization dose. We design Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) systems that hold USP <645> 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C, 500 ppb total organic carbon (TOC) and the endotoxin and microbial limits your risk assessment sets, at the washer inlet, and we hand over factory acceptance test (FAT) and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) records that fit an ISO 13485 quality system.

blocks.h: In a device plant, rinse water is part of a validated process
body: No standard sets one water grade for medical device manufacturing. ISO 13485:2016 asks you to control product cleanliness (7.5.2) and contamination (6.4.2), to validate any process whose output you cannot fully verify (7.5.6), and to maintain the infrastructure behind it (6.3). Cleaning is such a process, so the water at the end of it is part of your validation, and a water excursion is a cleaning deviation.

Three things set the grade: what the device contacts, how it is sterilized, and the release limits on the finished device. A non-sterile device for intact skin can be rinsed in PW. An implant, a blood-contacting device or anything for the central nervous system is usually rinsed in water with a written endotoxin limit, because endotoxin is heat stable and survives every common sterilization method. A device sterilized by radiation or ethylene oxide (EO) carries the bioburden its last rinse left, and that bioburden sets the dose.

Since 2 February 2026 the FDA Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR, 21 CFR 820) incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference. Health Canada licenses Class II to IV devices on an ISO 13485 certificate issued under the Medical Device Single Audit Program (MDSAP). One set of water system records can now answer both.

blocks.h: Where rinse water puts endotoxin and bioburden on devices, and what we design against
rows: Washer and ultrasonic tanks
Water sits warm in a tank between batches and grows biofilm the supply loop never sees
A sample point at the washer inlet and a drain-and-refill rule you can validate; supply sized so tanks refill fast
Short, high-flow draws
Several washers fill at once, loop pressure drops and the far end of the loop stagnates
Storage and pump sized to your washer fill profile, return flow monitored and alarmed
Ambient PW loops
Most device plants run PW at ambient temperature, where biofilm forms if sanitization lapses
Ozone or ultraviolet (UV) control with ozone removal proven before use, or hot water sanitization on a stated schedule
Dead legs and drops to cleanroom washers
Branches and long drops to points of use hold stagnant water
Branches to an L/D of 2 or less to ASME BPE, drops kept short and drainable
Point-of-use filters and ultrafilters
A filter or ultrafilter can be breached, or grow the biofilm it was meant to stop
Integrity testing, a change interval set from data and sampling downstream of the filter
Hoses, spray wands and sampling
Water picks up contamination after the outlet valve, then the result reads as a loop failure
Sampling procedures that match how production draws water, and investigation records that separate the two

blocks.h: How the systems connect in a device plant
blocks.caption: Reverse osmosis (RO) with electrodeionization (EDI) makes PW, stored and circulated in an ambient loop under ozone or UV control, or hot where the demand profile suits it. Final rinse points for implants and blood-contact devices take water through ultrafiltration or from a membrane WFI skid; general rinses and passivation lines take PW from the loop. A clean steam generator fed with PW serves in-house steam sterilizers. Monitoring and controls run across all of it, with audit-trailed records under 21 CFR Part 11.

blocks.h: Decisions to settle before the URS is approved

items.t: An endotoxin limit on PW, or WFI
items.d: Many device makers rinse in PW held to a written endotoxin limit, polished by ultrafiltration at the point of use. WFI is simpler to defend for CSF-contact devices. We work the rinse water limit back from your device limit and extraction volume, then compare both routes.
Water quality at the generator is not the water on your device. We put the specification and the sample point at the washer inlet, where your cleaning validation needs it.

items.t: Washer fill profile, not daily total
items.d: Washers and ultrasonic baths fill fast and then stop. Storage, pump and loop are sized from how many fill at once, how much and how fast.

Ambient loops with ozone suit most device plants and use less energy; they need ozone removal proven before use. A hot loop suits plants that also need WFI or rinse hot. We compare them on your demand.

items.t: A rinse endpoint you can measure
items.d: A final rinse validated to a conductivity or TOC endpoint at the washer drain gives you a release check on every cycle, not only during validation.

Feed temperature can swing from near freezing in winter to over 20 °C in summer, and some municipal supplies use chloramine. We size membranes at your coldest month and design chloramine removal ahead of the RO.

blocks.h: Adjacent use: water for hospital device reprocessing (MDRD)
body: Hospitals that reprocess reusable devices in a medical device reprocessing department (MDRD), or sterile processing department, work to different rules from device makers. In Canada that is CSA Z314, Canadian medical device reprocessing; in the United States, ANSI/AAMI ST108:2023, Water for the processing of medical devices, which replaced AAMI TIR34. ST108 sets categories for utility water, critical water for final rinse and steam generation, and steam. There is no ISO 13485 product release behind it, but the risk is the same: water left on an instrument goes into a patient.

The same RO and EDI platform we build for device makers can be built for hospital reprocessing water under CSA Z314, usually with duplex or N+1 redundancy because an MDRD cannot stop. blocks.h: Questions device engineering, validation and QA leads ask

items.q: Do we need WFI for our final rinse?
items.a: Only if your risk assessment says the rinse water must meet the WFI endotoxin limit, which is common for devices that contact cerebrospinal fluid. For most implants and blood-contact devices, PW with a written endotoxin limit and point-of-use ultrafiltration does the job at lower cost. We show the calculation from your device limit either way.

items.q: Our rinse water meets USP Purified Water. Is that enough for implant cleaning validation?
items.a: Not on its own. The USP PW monograph sets conductivity and TOC but no endotoxin limit, and its microbial level is guidance in USP <1231>, not a monograph limit. If endotoxin or bioburden on the device matters, write those limits into the water specification and sample at the washer inlet.

items.q: How does rinse water affect our radiation sterilization dose?
items.a: Your dose is set and audited from device bioburden measured to ISO 11737-1. A rise in rinse water bioburden shows up as higher device bioburden and can fail a dose audit under ISO 11137-2. Stable, trended rinse water is one of the cheapest ways to protect a validated dose.

items.q: What changed for our water system under the QMSR?
items.a: The FDA requirements now read as ISO 13485:2016 clauses: infrastructure, contamination control, process validation, calibration. If your water system already sits in an ISO 13485 system, the records are largely the same. We map our documents to those clauses so one package serves MDSAP, Health Canada and the FDA.

items.q: Is the water system validated or qualified?
items.a: Both words get used. Under ISO 13485 7.5.6 the cleaning process is validated; the water system that supplies it is qualified by IQ and OQ, with PQ evidence from routine sampling. We follow GHTF SG3/N99-10, the process validation guidance most device auditors know.

items.q: Is hospital reprocessing water the same as manufacturing rinse water?
items.a: No. Hospital MDRDs work to CSA Z314 and ANSI/AAMI ST108; device makers set their own specification under ISO 13485. The treatment platform overlaps. The hospital reprocessing section above sets out our scope.
